title: React: Add component metadata extraction via Volar-style LanguageService
body:
## What I did

Adds a new prop extraction engine (`react-component-meta`) that uses TypeScript's own LanguageService — the same API behind IDE autocomplete — to detect components and extract props. Instead of AST heuristics (react-docgen) or throwaway `ts.Program` per file (react-docgen-typescript), it maintains a persistent LanguageService with incremental updates.

The architecture mirrors [Vue Component Meta](https://github.com/vuejs/language-tools/tree/master/packages/component-meta) — built on `@volar/typescript` and `@volar/language-core`.

### Why

Neither existing engine works reliably on real design systems:

| # | Pattern | RD | RDT | RCM | Projects | Count |
|---|---------|-----|------|------|----------|-------|
| 1 | `polymorphicFactory()` | FAIL | OK | OK | Mantine | 133 |
| 2 | `export * as X from` + HOC | FAIL | FAIL | OK | Park UI | 29 |
| 3 | `styled(ark.div, recipe)` HOC | FAIL | OK | OK | Park UI | 17 |
| 4 | `React.FC<T.Props>` (namespace type import) | FAIL | OK | OK | Reshaped | 63 |
| 5 | `forwardRef() as PolymorphicForwardRefComponent` | Partial | FAIL | OK | Primer | 38 |
| 6 | `Object.assign(Component, { subs })` compound | FAIL | FAIL | OK | Primer | ~15 |
| 7 | `createComponent()` for Web Components | FAIL | OK | OK | Primer | ~5 |
| 8 | Discriminated union props | FAIL | OK | OK | Flowbite | 1 |
| 9 | Generic polymorphic forwardRef + cast | Partial | FAIL | OK | Flowbite | 1 |

### How it works

**Probe-free.** Instead of generating virtual files, the engine reads existing story files directly:

**Path 1 — JSX extraction (~95%):** `resolvePropsFromStoryFile()` — finds JSX elements in the story file that match the target component (CSF1 or CSF3 with `render`), then calls `checker.getResolvedSignature()` to extract the full props type. TypeScript resolves props the same way as autocompletion — polymorphic components with generic call signatures get instantiated with their default type parameter, giving correct concrete props.

**Path 2 — Component type fallback:** `resolvePropsFromComponentType()` — for args-only CSF3 stories with no JSX, inspects the component's type directly via `getCallSignatures()[0].parameters[0]`. Does NOT work for polymorphic/generic components (TS #61133).

We also tried **virtual probe files** with synthetic JSX to force `getResolvedSignature` on the fallback path — but injecting files into the TS program invalidates caches and hurts performance. Scanning real story files is much faster.

Both paths produce a `ts.Type` which is then serialized into `ComponentDoc` format by `serializeComponentDocs()`.

### Why Volar-style LanguageService

The naive approach (`ts.createProgram()` per request) means full TypeScript program creation on every dev server cycle — expensive for large projects like Mantine (9 tsconfig projects). Instead, we use `@volar/typescript` directly:

- **`ComponentMetaProject`** — one `LanguageService` per tsconfig (mirrors Volar's `TypeScriptProjectHost` + `createTypeScriptCheckerLanguageService`)
- **`ComponentMetaManager`** — manages multiple projects, routes component requests to the right tsconfig (mirrors Volar LS's `typescriptProject.ts`)
- **`projectVersion++` invalidation** — on file change events, bump the version counter. The LS compares file mtimes and only recompiles what changed
- **File watching** — `fs.watch` with debounce. Watchers are created lazily when projects are discovered
- **Shared mtime-based snapshots** — file reads are cached across projects via `@volar/language-core`'s `FileMap` (monorepo support — Mantine's 9 tsconfigs share one snapshot cache)
- **Background warmup** — after file change, `scheduleWarmup()` replays the last extraction so the cache is hot before the next request

### Architecture (Volar alignment)

| Concept | Vue Component Meta / Volar | This PR |
|---------|---------------------------|---------| 
| Per-tsconfig checker | `TypeScriptProjectHost` + `createLanguageServiceHost` | `ComponentMetaProject` |
| Multi-project manager | `typescriptProject.ts` | `ComponentMetaManager` |
| Language core | `@volar/language-core` `createLanguage()` | `@volar/language-core` `createLanguage()` |
| LS host | `@volar/typescript` `createLanguageServiceHost()` | `@volar/typescript` `createLanguageServiceHost()` |
| Component detection | Vue SFC parsing | JSX in story files + `isReactComponentType()` |
| Prop extraction | Template type narrowing | `getResolvedSignature()` on JSX / `getCallSignatures()` fallback |
| File snapshots | `FileMap` with mtime cache | `FileMap` with mtime cache |
| Invalidation | `projectVersion++` | `projectVersion++` |

### Other changes

- **`getComponentImports.ts`** — tracks JSX nesting depth per component, adds `member` field for member expressions (`Accordion.Root` → `member: "Root"`). Both react-docgen and react-docgen-typescript always run.
- **`generator.ts`** — prefers outermost JSX component (shallowest depth) instead of alphabetical order. `memberAccess` derived from `component.member` instead of regex scanning.
- **Bulk source exclusions** — extended to `.d.ts` files (catches generated type systems like Panda CSS `styled-system/`).

## Results

Tested on 5 design systems with published canary `0.0.0-pr-33914-sha-ba1d6f53`.

### Component Detection

| Project | Components | RD | RDT | **RCM** |
|---------|-----------|-----|------|------|
| Flowbite | 43 | 42 (98%) | 42 (98%) | **43 (100%)** |
| Reshaped | 63 | 0 (0%) | 63 (100%) | **63 (100%)** |
| Park UI | 54 | 8 (15%) | 25 (46%) | **54 (100%)** |
| Primer | 212 | 188 (89%) | 161 (76%) | **212 (100%)** |
| Mantine | 154 | 19 (12%) | 152 (99%) | **154 (100%)** |

**RCM: 526/526 — 100% detection across all 5 projects.**

### Props Extracted

| Project | RD | RDT | **RCM** |
|---------|-----|------|------|
| Flowbite | 282 | 308 | **321** |
| Reshaped | 0 | 827 | **842** |
| Park UI | 11 | 205 | **1,021** |
| Primer | 1,010 | 1,030 | **1,865** |
| Mantine | 535 | 12,382 | **10,292** |

Mantine RDT (12,382) > RCM (10,292) — RDT includes inherited HTML/DOM props (100+ `HTMLAttributes` per component). RCM's source filter (>30 props from a single `.d.ts`) keeps only meaningful props.

### Prop Quality (RCM = ground truth)

| Project | RD Recall | RD Precision | RDT Recall | RDT Precision |
|---------|-----------|--------------|------------|---------------|
| Flowbite | 94% | 98% | 97% | 98% |
| Reshaped | 0% | 0% | 98% | 100% |
| Park UI | 2% | 15% | 31% | 46% |
| Primer | 63% | 86% | 57% | 76% |
| Mantine | 11% | 12% | 98% | 84% |

Deep per-component validation: **RCM is a strict superset of both RD and RDT** on 4 out of 5 projects. On Mantine, the only gap is `.d.ts` style props (by design — in a user's project, Mantine is in `node_modules` and style props are correctly excluded). No engine ever found a prop that RCM incorrectly missed.

### Performance — Cold Start (build mode)

| Project | RD | RDT | **RCM** |
|---------|-----|------|------|
| Flowbite | 1,708ms | 1,999ms | **1,481ms** |
| Reshaped | 729ms | 1,859ms | **1,599ms** |
| Park UI | 812ms | **32,890ms** | 4,350ms |
| Primer | 2,394ms | 3,540ms | 3,397ms |
| Mantine | 5,180ms | 6,858ms | 9,387ms |

Cold start happens once. RCM is in the same ballpark as RDT — except Park UI where RDT takes **33 seconds** (Panda CSS types are deep + throwaway Program per file).

### Performance — Dev Mode (after file edit)

| Project | RD | RDT | **RCM** | **speedup vs RDT** |
|---------|-----|------|------|------|
| Flowbite | 1,591ms | 1,783ms | **27ms** | 66x |
| Reshaped | 694ms | 1,449ms | **18ms** | 81x |
| Park UI | 697ms | 40,553ms | **46ms** | **882x** |
| Primer | 2,190ms | 2,880ms | **41ms** | 70x |
| Mantine | 5,851ms | 8,698ms | **200ms** | 43x |

RD and RDT rebuild from scratch every time. RCM's LanguageService is persistent — **18–200ms after every edit** across all projects.

### File Invalidation (no story touch needed)

| Project | Edited file | Before | After edit | After revert |
|---------|--------|---:|---:|---:|
| Flowbite | `ListGroup.tsx` | 321 props | 322 (+1) ✅ | 321 ✅ |
| Reshaped | `Button.types.ts` | 842 props | 843 (+1) ✅ | 842 ✅ |
| Park UI | `button.tsx` | 1,021 props | 1,022 (+1) ✅ | 1,021 ✅ |
| Primer | `Button/types.ts` | 1,865 props | 1,875 (+10) ✅ | 1,865 ✅ |
| Mantine | `Button.tsx` | 10,292 props | 10,293 (+1) ✅ | 10,292 ✅ |

Only the component source file was edited — no story file touch needed. File watcher detects changes → bumps `projectVersion++` → LanguageService incrementally recompiles only affected files.

## Checklist for Contributors

### Testing

#### The changes in this PR are covered in the following automated tests:

- [ ] stories
- [x] unit tests
- [ ] integration tests
- [ ] end-to-end tests

- [ ] Add or update documentation reflecting your changes

      [MIGRATION.MD](https://github.com/storybookjs/storybook/blob/next/MIGRATION.md)

## Checklist for Maintainers

- [ ] When this PR is ready for testing, make sure to add `ci:normal`, `ci:merged` or `ci:daily` GH label to it to run a specific set of sandboxes. The particular set of sandboxes can be found in `code/lib/cli-storybook/src/sandbox-templates.ts`
- [ ] Make sure this PR contains **one** of the labels below:

  - `bug`: Internal changes that fixes incorrect behavior.
  - `maintenance`: User-facing maintenance tasks.
  - `dependencies`: Upgrading (sometimes downgrading) dependencies.
  - `build`: Internal-facing build tooling & test updates. Will not show up in release changelog.
  - `cleanup`: Minor cleanup style change. Will not show up in release changelog.
  - `documentation`: Documentation **only** changes. Will not show up in release changelog.
  - `feature request`: Introducing a new feature.
  - `BREAKING CHANGE`: Changes that break compatibility in some way with current major version.
  - `other`: Changes that don't fit in the above categories.

   </details>

#### Manual testing

Tested on 5 design systems (Flowbite, Reshaped, Park UI, Primer, Mantine) with published canary. See results tables in the PR description above.

kasperpeulen
comments.body: Not a bug — this matches the original Volar LS pattern exactly ([source](https://github.com/volarjs/volar.js/blob/master/packages/language-server/lib/project/typescriptProject.ts)). Volar intentionally only cleans `rootTsConfigs` when a project was created for that config. If no project exists, the stale path is harmless: `searchedDirs.clear()` fires on every config change, forcing a re-scan that uses `sys.fileExists()` before adding configs.

## `fs.watch(..., { recursive: true })` platform support

- **Supported:** **macOS** and **Windows** only. ([nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v9.9.0/docs/api/fs.html?utm_source=openai))  
- **Not supported:** **Linux** (and other Unix-like platforms such as BSD/SunOS/AIX). On these platforms, Node’s docs explicitly call out that recursive watching is not available. ([nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v9.9.0/docs/api/fs.html?utm_source=openai))

## Compatibility notes (important caveats)

- `fs.watch` behavior is **not fully consistent across OSes** because it depends on OS-specific backends (e.g., **inotify** on Linux, **ReadDirectoryChangesW** on Windows, **FSEvents** for directories on macOS). ([nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v9.9.0/docs/api/fs.html?utm_source=openai))  
- Watching can be **unreliable or not work** on some environments like **network filesystems** or certain virtualization/shared-folder setups. ([nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v9.11.0/docs/api/fs.html?utm_source=openai))  

## If you need recursive watching on Linux

- Common approach: use a library such as **chokidar**, which implements recursive directory watching in a cross-platform way (including by creating watchers per subdirectory where needed). ([npmjs.com](https://www.npmjs.com/package/chokidar/v/3.0.0?utm_source=openai))

**`fs.watch({ recursive: true })` silently fails on Linux; implement platform-aware fallback or explicit error handling.**

The `recursive` option is only supported on macOS and Windows. On Linux, the call throws `ERR_FEATURE_UNAVAILABLE_ON_PLATFORM`, but the catch block at line 489–491 logs at DEBUG level only and returns silently. This means users on Linux will silently lose file change detection for the component manifest with no clear indication of failure. Either switch to a cross-platform library like chokidar, implement a recursive watcher fallback for unsupported platforms, or log a clear warning at INFO level when recursive watching is unavailable.

**Remove optional chaining and fix type safety violation.**

The optional chaining on `typescript.isTypeAssertionExpression?.(node)` is unnecessary—the API exists in TypeScript 4.0+ and the project requires TypeScript 5.9.3. All other type guard calls in this file (e.g., `isCallExpression`, `isAsExpression`, `isParenthesizedExpression`) use direct calls without optional chaining. Additionally, the `(node as any).expression` cast violates TypeScript strict mode, which is enabled per coding guidelines. Use proper typing: `(node as ts.TypeAssertion).expression`.

comments.body:
_⚠️ Potential issue_ | _🟠 Major_

**Handle CSF read/parse failures per entry to avoid aborting the full manifest run.**

A single `cachedReadFileSync` or `loadCsf(...).parse()` failure here currently rejects the whole `manifests()` call instead of isolating the failure to one component.



<details>
<summary>Suggested hardening</summary>

```diff
-        const storyFile = cachedReadFileSync(absoluteImportPath, 'utf-8') as string;
-        const csf = loadCsf(storyFile, { makeTitle: () => entry.title }).parse();
+        let storyFile: string;
+        let csf: ReturnType<ReturnType<typeof loadCsf>['parse']>;
+        try {
+          storyFile = cachedReadFileSync(absoluteImportPath, 'utf-8') as string;
+          csf = loadCsf(storyFile, { makeTitle: () => entry.title }).parse();
+        } catch (e) {
+          invariant(e instanceof Error);
+          return {
+            manifest: {
+              id: entry.id.split('--')[0],
+              name: entry.title.split('/').at(-1)!.replace(/\s+/g, ''),
+              path: storyFilePath,
+              stories: [],
+              import: '',
+              jsDocTags: {},
+              error: { name: e.name, message: `${e.message}\n\n${entry.importPath}` },
+            } satisfies ReactComponentManifest,
+          };
+        }
```
</details>

<details>
<summary>🤖 Prompt for AI Agents</summary>

```
Verify each finding against the current code and only fix it if needed.

In `@code/renderers/react/src/componentManifest/generator.ts` around lines 229 -
237, Wrap the per-entry file read and CSF parse (the logic that computes
storyFilePath, absoluteImportPath, storyFile = cachedReadFileSync(...), and csf
= loadCsf(...).parse()) in a try/catch so a single failure doesn't reject the
whole manifests() run; on error log the entry identifier (e.g., entry.title or
entry.importPath) and the error, skip processing that entry (do not add its data
to the manifest output), and continue the loop. Ensure you catch both IO and
parse errors and keep the rest of the manifest generation unchanged.
```

</details>

comments.body:
_⚠️ Potential issue_ | _🟠 Major_

**`reactComponentMeta` extraction is unintentionally skipped when docgen is missing.**

The early `!hasDocgen` return does not include `componentMetaCtx`, so those entries never reach the manager extraction path, even when `component.path` is available.



<details>
<summary>Suggested fix</summary>

```diff
-        const hasDocgen = component?.reactDocgen || component?.reactDocgenTypescript;
+        const componentMetaCtx: ComponentMetaContext | undefined = component?.path
+          ? {
+              componentPath: component.path,
+              importName: component.importName,
+              importId: component.importId,
+              storyFilePath: absoluteImportPath,
+              memberAccess: component.member,
+            }
```

Can't use memfs here — `ComponentMetaProject` passes `typescript.sys` directly into Volar's `createLanguageServiceHost`, and the TS LanguageService needs to resolve real `@types/react`, `lib.d.ts` etc. from `node_modules`. That's why fixtures live under the monorepo root (so module resolution walks up and finds them).

The `../../../../..` is fragile though. Alternatives:
- Use `os.tmpdir()` + explicit `typeRoots` pointing at monorepo's `node_modules/@types` in the test tsconfig
- Use a `findUp` to locate the monorepo root instead of counting `..`
- Inject a custom `sys` that overlays memfs on real fs (memfs for test files, real fs fallback for node_modules) — bigger refactor

The react renderer's vitest setup mocks `node:fs` with memfs. Using `fs.mkdirSync` etc. here would write to the in-memory filesystem, which TypeScript's LanguageService can't see — `ts.sys` captured the real `fs` at import time before mocks were applied. So all test file I/O goes through `ts.sys` to stay on the real filesystem.

comments.author: kasperpeulen

Yeah, I agree this API shape is a bit awkward.

The main reason it looks like this is that Claude kept it aligned with the existing RDT API, which I think is fine for now for compatibility.

In practice that means `defaultValue` is treated as “serialized source text if present, otherwise null”, so:

- no default found -> `defaultValue: null`
- `= 'hello'` -> `defaultValue: { value: "'hello'" }`
- `= null` -> `defaultValue: { value: 'null' }`
- `= { a: 1 }` -> `defaultValue: { value: '{ a: 1 }' }`

I don’t think this is the ideal long-term shape if we were designing it fresh. At some point it would probably make sense to unify this with some more standard/default-value schema instead of inheriting the RDT compatibility shape. But for this PR, keeping the same API felt like the safer tradeoff.

comments.author: kasperpeulen

I think this is a good direction, but it’s not as straightforward as it first looks.

Props can come in through `extends`, intersections, unions, utility types, and those chains can be several levels deep. The filtered props also often point at lower-level internal React types (`HTMLAttributes`, `DOMAttributes`, etc.), not necessarily the exact top-level type reference the user wrote.

So there’s definitely room to improve this later, but I don’t think there’s a trivial “if props were filtered, just use that name for `extends`” rule that will be reliably correct across real-world cases.
